title: Gather Victim Org Information: Identify Roles
shortTitle: Gather Victim Org Information: Identify Roles
summary: This sub-technique covers collection about the identities inside a victim organisation and what each person is able to reach. Adversaries map names to job titles, teams, and responsibilities, then infer access: who approves payments, who administers directory or cloud systems, who handles sensitive projects or executive support. Sources are mostly open, including staff pages, professional networking profiles, conference talks, public code repositories, and naming patterns visible in email addresses or document metadata, with phishing for information used to fill gaps and previously leaked data reused where available. The output directly shapes targeted phishing, business email compromise, and credential attacks, and it identifies accounts whose compromise yields disproportionate access. On the defensive side, mail gateway logs, authentication records, multi-factor authentication prompts that were not initiated by the user, and directory enumeration queries are the useful evidence, and the hardest judgement is separating normal recruiting or sales research from deliberate enumeration of privileged roles.

beginner.definition: This sub-technique is about finding out who does what inside a target organisation. It covers names, job titles, and what each person can access. The attacker wants to know who holds the keys.
beginner.whyItMatters: Phishing works better when it reaches the right person. A message to an accountant about an unpaid invoice is believable. A message to a helpdesk worker about a password reset looks normal. Attackers also look for people with administrator rights, because those accounts are worth far more than an ordinary one.
howItWorks: The attacker lists employee names and job titles from your website and staff profiles.
They study public talks and articles to learn which teams own which systems.
They guess email addresses from the pattern your organisation appears to use.
They look for people who mention administrator tools, finance work, or executive support.
They build a short list of targets who can approve payments or change access.
They then write messages that fit each person's daily work and habits.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital at night. A visitor walks to the reception desk and asks which ward handles heart surgery. The receptionist answers, because helping people find wards is part of the job. The visitor then asks for the name of the nurse in charge. That answer is also given freely. By morning the visitor knows exactly who to page and what to say. Nothing they did was forbidden, because they simply asked the right questions in the right order. Identifying roles works the same way. The attacker learns who holds authority, then uses that name to sound trustworthy.
takeaways: Job titles and team pages tell attackers who can approve money or change access.
Use multi-factor authentication on every account that can approve payments or administer systems.
Train the people most likely to be impersonated to verify unusual requests before acting.

objectives: Explain what role identification collects and how it supports targeted social engineering.
Identify open sources that reveal names, titles, and team responsibilities.
Describe how email naming patterns are inferred and abused.
Recognise authentication and mail telemetry that indicates targeting of specific staff.
Distinguish legitimate business research from deliberate enumeration of privileged roles.
